title: Leadership
author: The Good Boss
summary: The author introduces the Hawthorne Effect through a personal story of inheriting a disengaged team whose performance improved not through process changes but through consistent managerial presence. The Hawthorne Effect traces to 1920s experiments at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works plant, where researchers found that worker productivity improved regardless of the specific change made, suggesting the knowledge of being observed was the active variable. The essay reframes this for contemporary leaders across three layers: behavioral change under observation, the distorting effect of leader presence on authentic team behavior, and the implications for building trust and psychological safety. Though subsequent researchers complicated the original findings, the core behavioral insight has persisted: observation and attention shape human behavior in measurable ways. The author's practical advice is to shift from watching as inspection to being present as investment.
points: The Hawthorne Effect's core finding is counterintuitive: what changed worker behavior was not the specific improvement made to conditions but the simple fact that workers knew someone was paying attention to them.

Leader presence creates a double-edged dynamic: the attention can improve short-term performance while simultaneously masking what team performance actually looks like without observation, making accurate assessment difficult.

Subsequent researchers complicated the original Hawthorne data, but the core behavioral insight has held across decades of organizational research: observation and attention shape human behavior in measurable and predictable ways.

The practical leadership implication is to distinguish between watching as inspection, which signals distrust, and being present as investment, which signals interest; both involve attention but produce very different behavioral responses.

Leaders who shift from inspection-mode presence to trust-based presence tend to get more accurate pictures of actual team capacity because team members stop performing for the observer and start operating normally.

When I took over, I was sceptical, and nervous at the same time. I didn't know what I was getting into, so I decided to do something simple: I started showing up. I didn't overhaul the process, but simply started being there, whether in meetings, working sessions, etc.

Within a few weeks, I observed a change: the work quality picked up, and so did the energy in the team meetings. And I found myself wondering: was this me, or was something else going on? What changed was that the team knew someone was paying attention.

What the Hawthorne Effect Really Is The Hawthorne Effect traces back to a series of experiments conducted in the 1920s and 1930s at the Hawthorne Works, a Western Electric factory near Chicago. Researchers set out to study whether changes in physical working conditions, such as lighting levels, break schedules, working hours, etc. Productivity improved almost regardless of what change they made.

The results were consistently positive, no matter the direction of the change. The conclusion researchers eventually Page 1 drew was striking: it wasn't the changes themselves that were driving the improvement. It was the fact that workers knew they were being observed.

The Hawthorne Effect, in its simplest form, is this: people change their behavior when they know they are being watched. I do want to note that subsequent researchers have debated the original findings and their interpretation, and the data from those studies was messier than the clean narrative suggests. But the core behavioral insight has helped up over the decades of organizational research and real-world leadership experience: attention shapes behavior.
